overview: Chen was the last of the Southern Dynasties, ruling from Jiankang, today’s Nanjing, in 557-589. It inherited a battered and reduced part of the Liang realm, then fought northern rivals for the Huai River region. The atlas index has the historical dates, but its border feature continues to 600 and reuses an oversized outline also assigned to Southern Qi. That shape overstates Chen’s reach and cannot show its changing frontiers.

periods.title: Foundation and contested succession
periods.summary: Chen Baxian replaces Liang in 557. His successors face local military powers and a struggle within the ruling family.

periods.title: Emperor Xuan’s campaigns
periods.summary: Chen Xu rules as Emperor Xuan while armies fight for territory north of the Yangtze.

periods.title: The final court
periods.summary: Chen Shubao succeeds his father; Sui conquers Jiankang in 589.

sections.title: A southern court and its changing frontiers

items.text: Chen’s emperors governed a smaller realm than their Liang predecessors. Western territories had already fallen to northern powers, while local military leaders retained considerable independence. Securing obedience inside the realm was as important as defending its borders.

In 573, Emperor Xuan sent Wu Mingche north against Northern Qi. His armies recovered the Huainan region, giving Chen a stronger position beyond the Yangtze. This was a significant expansion for a state that had begun with a much reduced territory.

The advantage did not last. After Northern Zhou conquered Northern Qi, Wu Mingche attacked Pengcheng in 578. Zhou forces cut his route behind him, and his retreat ended in defeat and capture. Boats could carry an army along rivers, but an enemy controlling its way home could turn that strength into a trap.

sections.title: Buying things, family obligations and learning

items.text: Early Chen markets used a jumble of coins inherited from Liang, including tiny pieces nicknamed goose-eye money. Historical evidence also describes grain and silk used in exchange. A family’s useful stores could therefore double as payment: food and cloth mattered alongside metal cash.

The new six-zhu coin of 579 was initially valued at ten five-zhu coins. Its official exchange rate was later reduced to one for one. Historian Chen Yanliang uses this reversal to explain unstable money under Chen. Imagine checking prices while the government changes what your coins are supposed to buy.

One family faced a painful border problem: their father’s coffin remained in Northern Zhou while a son tried to retrieve it. The Book of Chen records officials allowing relatives still in Chen to finish formal mourning, so marriages would not be postponed indefinitely. Burial could be arranged later if the coffin returned.

Zheng Zhuo, a scholar whose career spanned Liang and Chen, copied commentaries despite poverty and worn brushes. The later history says he ate vegetable food and cooled his chest with melons when teaching made him feel overheated. Then he returned to reciting. This is one memorable scholar’s reported habit, not a recommended remedy.

Learning also happened at home. Zhang Ji arranged a garden with hills, ponds, flowers and fruit trees, where he taught the Changes, Laozi and Zhuangzi. His named pupils included Buddhist monks and a Daoist. The Book of Chen preserves this unusually vivid picture of a teacher’s household and its circle of students.

Medical learning could run through families. The Book of Sui says Xu Zhizang’s grandfather studied remedies when his own mother became ill, then urged his sons to learn them. Xu became known for medicine and served the Chen court before continuing under Sui. This is evidence for one medical family, rather than universal access to treatment.

An excavated epitaph dates the tomb of general Huang Faqu to 576. That gives archaeologists a firmly dated Chen example against which to compare less informative burials. The shapes of tomb chambers and their objects can become clues when another tomb has lost its owner’s name.

The large Lingshan tomb contained a green-glazed lotus vessel and stone figures measuring 46 and 64 centimeters high. These elaborate burial furnishings suggest a very important owner. Archaeologist Wei Zheng argues that it probably belonged to Emperor Wen, but that identification remains an interpretation, not an inscription naming the emperor.

Decorated bricks can carry clues about migration as well as art. Wei Zheng connects some late southern tomb images around Nanjing with traditions farther up the Yangtze. He proposes that people fleeing upheaval helped carry these designs downstream. The proposed link draws together objects, their distribution and written migration accounts.

The Smithsonian’s Chen coin is only 25 millimeters across and 1 millimeter thick. It is catalogued as copper and dated to 579. Such a small object preserves evidence of government, metalworking and everyday exchange together. An empire’s history can sometimes fit in the palm of a hand.

sections.title: Reading Chen writing and following its legacy

items.text: The coin’s seal-script legend is 太貨六銖, shown here in modern traditional type. Modern Mandarin reads tài huò liù zhū; the Smithsonian translates it as “Large Coin Six Zhu.” Its catalogue prints the simplified forms 太货六铢. This is a genuine period coin inscription, while the typeface and pronunciation guide are modern ways of helping us read it.

The Book of Chen was completed under the Tang, drawing on earlier records and work by a father and son, Yao Cha and Yao Silian. Modern editors compare its text with excavated inscriptions. Huang Faqu’s damaged epitaph helped identify the tomb, and its wording then helped editors check the received history. Books and archaeology can correct each other.

Conquest changed Jiankang, but its inhabitants did not simply disappear. A recent study argues that Sui initially ordered destruction and planned to move residents away, then changed course after southern rebellion. Civilian houses and markets survived under the revised administration, helping sustain the city’s later life.

ending.text: Sui armies captured Jiankang and Chen Shubao in 589, ending the dynasty and the long division between northern and southern courts. Families, learning and urban life continued under new rulers. The border feature’s 600 endpoint is imported map coverage, not an eleven-year extension of Chen rule.
